newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel, Tietmeyer to meet on reserve revaluation.
newsitem.headline: Waigel, Tietmeyer to meet on reserve revaluation.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel and Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer were set to meet on Thursday to find a compromise over plans to revalue central bank reserves to help Bonn fill holes in its budget.

After comments from Waigel on Wednesday, it was widely expected that the two men would meet in Bonn on Thursday afternoon, but neither the Bundesbank nor the Finance Ministry would comment on details of the planned meeting.

The government and the central bank are thought to be near a compromise in which the Bundesbank would agree to a revised revaluation plan that would allow it to transfer a portion of the profits to Bonn, but not in 1997.
"We are on the way to resolving the issue over the revaluation of the Bundesbank's reserves," Waigel said on Wednesday.
Tietmeyer also said on Wednesday that he expected to reach a final agreement "very soon" when he meets Waigel this week.

Sources close to the Bundesbank have indicated the central bank might be willing to revalue its dollar reserves to between 1.50-1.55 marks, up from current book rate of 1.36 marks, but still well below the current market exchange rate.
The sources also said there was no longer any discussion of revaluing the central bank's gold reserves before the start of monetary union in 1999.

The meeting on Thursday aims to end a bitter row between the fiercely independent central bank and Chancellor Helmut Kohl's beleaguered coalition over tapping Bundesbank reserves in its bid to qualify for Europe's single currency.

Waigel stunned financial markets last month when he announced that the government was planning to seek a change in the law regulating the Bundesbank that would have allowed it to revalue the central bank's gold and currency reserves, which are priced well below market value.

The move would have caused the Bundesbank to transfer billions in realised profits to the federal government, aiding Bonn in its efforts to cap mounting budget deficits, pay off debt and come closer to meeting the fiscal targets outlined in the Maastricht treaty on European monetary union (EMU).

But it immediately backfired. Bundesbank council members came out in full force denouncing the grab for central bank gold as an outright attack on the bank's near sacrosanct independence and a damaging precedent for monetary union.

Germany, which had chastised other countries in Europe for resorting to creative accounting to make the grade for EMU, was suddenly suspected of resorting to hectic last-ditch efforts to put its own house in order.
Facing a storm of protest, Waigel quickly retreated, but even Bundesbank officials have acknowleged that the affair has probably done lasting damage to the central bank's image abroad.
